blocks.text: Verse 25: And I will restore to you the years that the arbe, jelek, chasil and gazam have eaten, my great army, which I sent among you.] In verses 22, 23 and 24 the Prophet, in God's name, promises the exact opposite of all the threats that had gone before: namely, that the pastures of the wilderness will grow green, the trees will bear their fruit, and the fig tree and the vine will yield their strength, since God will send down abundant rain, both early and late, at the proper time; and the threshing floors will be filled with grain, and the vats of the winepresses will overflow with new wine and oil. Thus the years will be restored [col. 482] to the wretched Jews, that is, the yearly produce which the four kinds of locusts had consumed: not one kind in each year, as we have pointed out, but all at the same time, succeeding one another. For how many years this plague afflicted Canaan we simply do not know. We know only that the Jews were afflicted by these locusts both severely and for several years, God thus punishing the stubborn and those who despised his name. That is why he calls the locusts his great army. So do the Arabs as well. Thus in Damir a law is cited as enacted and promulgated by Muhammad: لا تقتلوا الجراد فانها جند [III, 319] الله الاعظم [lā taqtulū al-jarād fa-innahā jund Allāh al-aʿẓam] You shall not kill locusts, for they are the army of the most great God. Not to mention the tale told by Ibn-Omar, that locusts fell into the hands of that same pseudo-Prophet with this inscription on their wings: نحن جند الله الاكبر [naḥnu jund Allāh al-akbar] We are the army of the most great God.

Those who twist into a mystical sense what has so far been adduced from Joel about the locusts make a great show of objecting that nothing is found in the histories of Kings and Chronicles about so severe an invasion of locusts into Judaea, or about the famine that followed it. Jerome: For neither the history of Kings nor of Chronicles relates it; and certainly, had it happened, Scripture would never have been silent, just as we read of the famine of three years and six months under Elias. Abarbanel on Joel, Question 4: If the famine and the locusts were so severe, whether in the days of Joram, son of Ahab, and in the days of Elisha, or in the time of Manasseh, when, according to the Seder Olam, Joel, Nahum and Habakkuk are said to have prophesied, the question is why no mention of this is made in the books of Kings. Or, if that very point is disputed, why did Jeremiah not mention it, who reports many things of no great importance? But neither in the books of Chronicles, where things are narrated more fully, does a single word about this occur, which is very remarkable. I reply that the sacred writers did not set themselves the task of reporting how often God afflicted Judaea with famine. Indeed, if the whole of Scripture is gone through from beginning to end, it will be found that the history of a famine is nowhere recounted except in passing, as an appendix, so to speak, to some other narrative. Thus in Gen. XII, 10. and XXVI, 1. a severe famine in the land of Canaan is reported under Abraham and Isaac, so that we might know why the former went to Egypt and the latter to Palestine [Philistia, Gen 26:1]. And in the forty-first chapter of Genesis Moses describes the seven-year famine that Joseph had foretold in order to pave the way for the marvellous histories of Joseph and his brothers, and of the harsh servitude of the Israelites in Egypt, from which God delivered them with a strong hand and an outstretched arm. In the whole book of Judges there is no history of a famine. Yet at the beginning of the book of Ruth it is told that Elimelech, a Bethlehemite, withdrew to the land of Moab on account of a famine that raged in Judaea under the judges. Likewise, because it concerned us to know how, once the family of Saul had been cut off, the kingdom of David was established, the second book of Samuel, chapter 21, deals with a three-year famine that could not be stopped except by crucifying seven men of Saul's line. Again, the histories of famine under the prophets Elias and Elisha, 1 Reg. XVIII, 2. and 2 Reg. IV, 38. and VIII, 1., are reported because of the miracles they performed on that account. Finally, Luke touches on the famine that occurred under Claudius in a single brief word, only to show that it had been foretold by Agabus, and that it gave the Christians of Antioch occasion to send alms [III, 320] to their brethren in Jerusalem. Apart from those cited, no other history of a famine is to be found in either Testament. Therefore, since in a history of four thousand years so little is reported on this subject, and that only in passing and for the sake of something else, why should [col. 483] we be surprised that the history of the famine which Joel had foretold has been passed over?
